canonical_statement: Does a QCD critical point exist in the temperature–baryon-chemical-potential phase diagram, and if it does exist, what are its critical temperature and density, as established by a first-principles study based on QCD?
definitions: Quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the fundamental theory of the strong interaction, is expected to exhibit a rich phase structure as temperature $T$ and baryon chemical potential $\mu_B$ (which controls net baryon density) are varied. At $\mu_B = 0$, first-principles lattice QCD simulations have established that the transition from hadronic matter to the quark-gluon plasma is a smooth analytic crossover at a pseudocritical temperature $T_c \approx 155\text{--}158$ MeV, not a true phase transition. Many phenomenological models and several QCD-based functional studies predict that at sufficiently large $\mu_B$ this crossover strengthens into a line of first-order phase transitions, which must then terminate at a critical endpoint — the QCD critical point — generically expected to lie in the three-dimensional Ising ($Z_2$) universality class, like the endpoint of the liquid-gas coexistence line of water.

The obstacle to a first-principles settlement is the fermion sign problem. In lattice QCD the partition function is evaluated by Monte Carlo importance sampling over gauge configurations, weighted by the fermion determinant. At nonzero real quark chemical potential the Euclidean action becomes complex, the determinant loses positivity, and importance sampling is no longer applicable. All existing workarounds — reweighting, Taylor expansion in $\mu_B/T$, analytic continuation from imaginary chemical potential, canonical (fixed-baryon-number) formulations, complex Langevin evolution, and Lefschetz thimble methods — either are limited to small $\mu_B/T$ or lose reliability precisely in the low-temperature, high-density region where a critical point would reside. Nagata's 2022 review (Prog. Part. Nucl. Phys. 127, 103991) documents this situation and states that even the existence of the critical point is not established.

The unresolved target is the conditional two-part question posed by the source review: establish from first principles whether a QCD critical point exists in the $T$–$\mu_B$ phase diagram, and, if it does, determine its critical temperature and density. 'First-principles' means a controlled calculation based on QCD itself — for example a lattice or functional-QCD computation with quantified systematic and statistical uncertainties — as opposed to phenomenological model estimates, which the source explicitly says cannot settle the question. Post-2022 literature has sharpened constraints (a continuum-extrapolated lattice equation-of-state analysis excludes a critical point at $\mu_B < 450$ MeV at the $2\sigma$ level under its continuation ansatz, and RHIC BES-II measurements narrow the experimentally viable region) without resolving the question.
scope: The existence or non-existence of the QCD critical point and, if it exists, the first-principles determination of its critical temperature and density on the QCD phase diagram; the source review documents that this remains open because the sign problem at nonzero quark chemical potential defeats importance sampling and undermines current methods precisely in the relevant low-temperature, high-density region.
aliases: Critical point of the QCD phase diagram

authoritative_formulation.citation: K. Nagata, Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems, Prog. Part. Nucl. Phys. 127, 103991 (2022), arXiv:2108.12423, Sec. 1.1.1
authoritative_formulation.exact_excerpt: However, the QCD critical point has not been discovered so far. Although there are many phenomenological studies regarding the QCD critical point, the location of the critical point on the phase diagram is not known. Even the very existence is not established. The first-principle study based on QCD is needed to establish the existence or non-existence of the QCD critical point, and if it does exist, to determine the critical temperature and density.

formulation_change.rationale: No major later progress was found that resolves or definitively narrows the source question. Post-2022 results constrain the critical-point region — the Borsanyi et al. 2025 continuum-extrapolated lattice equation-of-state analysis excludes a critical point at $\mu_B < 450$ MeV only at the $2\sigma$ level under a specific constant-entropy-density continuation ansatz, and STAR BES-II measurements narrow the viable experimental region with baseline-model-dependent significance — but neither settles existence even within the constrained regions, other lattice analyses (multipoint Pade, Lee-Yang edge searches) report candidate signals, and the question remains open in its full source generality. Canonical title, statement, scope, and answer types are therefore frozen exactly as received from Triage.

literature_treatment: Post-2022 literature across all three fronts treats the same core as open. On the lattice front, the Wuppertal-Budapest collaboration's improved continuum-extrapolated equation of state (arXiv:2502.10267, 2025) searches for the onset of first-order behavior along contours of constant entropy density from imaginary to real chemical potential and excludes a critical point at $\mu_B < 450$ MeV only at the $2\sigma$ level, explicitly leaving the higher-density region undecided; companion efforts (multipoint Pade approximants by Clarke et al., PRD 112, L091504 (2025); Lee-Yang edge singularity searches in high-statistics data, arXiv:2502.03211) continue to hunt for a signal rather than reporting closure. Functional QCD methods (fRG/DSE) continue to predict candidate critical-endpoint locations but with acknowledged truncation dependence, so they do not constitute a controlled first-principles determination. On the experimental front, STAR's precision BES-II net-proton fluctuation measurements (PRL 135, 142301 (2025), arXiv:2504.00817) find deviations from non-critical baselines at the $2\text{--}5\sigma$ level around $\sqrt{s_{NN}} \approx 19.6$ GeV and are publicly summarized as ruling out a critical point in the regions accessed at top RHIC and LHC energies while leaving lower energies open — narrowing, not closing, the search. Review-level treatments (Aarts et al., Prog. Part. Nucl. Phys. 133, 104070 (2023)) confirm that no sign-problem method yet provides the final solution. No later work claims a controlled first-principles establishment, exclusion over the full relevant region, or rigorous no-go result.
status_rationale: A systematic same-core web audit (the LKM/Gaia route was unavailable in this environment, a stated coverage limitation) was run across the canonical statement and aliases with closure-oriented queries, covering lattice QCD, functional methods, and the experimental BES-II program through August 2026. Every inspected item treats existence and location as undecided: the strongest lattice result is a $2\sigma$, ansatz-dependent regional exclusion; the strongest experimental result is a baseline-dependent deviation, not a discovery; functional predictions are truncation-dependent; and 2023–2026 reviews and status reports continue to list the critical point as an open problem. This constitutes continuing active treatment of the identical question with no credible closure, justifying still_open with likely_open at high confidence. The residual uncertainty is not about whether closure has been claimed — it clearly has not — but only about completeness of coverage of very recent preprints, which the 2026 items inspected mitigate.
checked_through: 2026-08 (lattice, functional-QCD, and experimental heavy-ion literature inspected through August 2026, including 2025–2026 BES-II publications and 2025–2026 lattice critical-endpoint searches)
surviving_open_core: The full source question survives: establish by a first-principles QCD study whether a critical point exists in the $T$–$\mu_B$ phase diagram, and, if it exists, determine its critical temperature and density with controlled uncertainties. The only refinement to record is contextual, not a reformulation: the region $\mu_B < 450$ MeV is now excluded at $2\sigma$ by one lattice continuation ansatz and the high-energy-collision region is experimentally disfavored, so the live target concentrates at moderate-to-large $\mu_B$ — but existence remains unestablished everywhere, and no definitive regional closure has been accepted by the community.
importance_motivation: This is one of the central open problems of strong-interaction physics, posed verbatim in a standard review (Nagata 2022) and echoed as a priority by the 2023 US Nuclear Science Long Range Plan and 2023–2026 status reports. The audited later literature confirms the problem is not only open but actively hunted by major programs (RHIC BES-II fixed-target running, FAIR/CBM planned for the late 2020s, Wuppertal-Budapest and multipoint-Pade lattice efforts), with 2025 results sharpening rather than settling it. A first-principles answer would fix the qualitative structure of the QCD phase diagram and redirect or vindicate a large international experimental program, which squarely justifies the high-importance assignment and the audit depth applied.
scientific_significance_rationale: Solving this problem would fix the qualitative structure of the QCD phase diagram at finite baryon density — whether a first-order transition line terminating in a critical endpoint exists at all — which is currently unknown from first principles. A positive answer with quantified critical temperature and density would (a) give heavy-ion collision programs (RHIC Beam Energy Scan, FAIR, NICA) a first-principles target to aim experimental searches at, replacing model-dependent extrapolations; (b) constrain the equation of state of dense baryonic matter relevant to neutron-star structure and mergers; and (c) require a demonstrably controlled method for the finite-density sign problem, a capability that would transfer to other sign-problem-afflicted theories (dense matter systems, real-time dynamics, some condensed-matter models). A rigorous exclusion or no-go result would be comparably consequential: it would redirect a major experimental search program and reshape the accepted phase diagram. The score is 9 rather than 10 because the deliverable is a specific structural feature of one theory's phase diagram rather than a bound or mechanism of universal scope, though the methodological spillover is substantial.
consequences_of_progress: A first-principles establishment with location would: fix the accepted topology of the QCD phase diagram; convert the experimental critical-point search (STAR fixed-target, FAIR/CBM, NICA) from an open scan into a targeted measurement around a computed $(T_E, \mu_B^E)$; provide a controlled dense-QCD equation of state input for neutron-star physics; and deliver a validated sign-problem methodology transferable to other complex-action theories. A controlled exclusion or rigorous no-go result would redirect experimental priorities toward other phase-diagram structure (e.g., quarkyonic or color-superconducting matter) and force revision of the standard phase-diagram picture used across nuclear physics. Either branch changes concrete scientific decisions about running and planned facilities.
current_best_result: No first-principles determination exists. Strongest current constraints: (1) Borsanyi et al. 2025 (arXiv:2502.10267), a continuum-extrapolated lattice equation of state extended via constant-entropy-density contours from imaginary chemical potential under strangeness neutrality, excludes a critical point at $\mu_B < 450$ MeV at the $2\sigma$ level within its ansatz. (2) STAR BES-II precision (net-)proton cumulant measurements (PRL 135, 142301 (2025), arXiv:2504.00817) exclude critical-point behavior in the region accessed at top RHIC and LHC energies and show $2\text{--}5\sigma$ deviations from non-critical baselines near $\sqrt{s_{NN}} \approx 19.6$ GeV that no existing model fully reproduces. (3) Functional QCD (fRG/DSE) studies yield candidate critical-endpoint locations, e.g. around $T \approx 100\text{--}120$ MeV, $\mu_B \approx 600\text{--}650$ MeV, but with uncontrolled truncation dependence. (4) Multipoint Pade (Clarke et al. 2025) and Lee-Yang edge analyses yield candidate signals or bounds depending on assumptions. None of these constitutes a controlled first-principles answer to existence plus location.
expected_result: A correct final submission is a first-principles determination, faithful to the source's conditional two-part question. Branch 1 (existence established): a controlled QCD-based calculation demonstrating a critical endpoint in the temperature–baryon-chemical-potential phase diagram, reporting its critical temperature and density with documented statistical and systematic uncertainties (including continuum and finite-volume control appropriate to the method used) and explicit evidence that the sign problem at nonzero chemical potential is controlled rather than assumed away. Branch 2 (existence excluded): a controlled first-principles calculation excluding a critical point in the relevant region of the phase diagram, with the region of exclusion and its uncertainties stated. Branch 3 (rigorous no-go): a proof-level result establishing non-existence (or constraining existence) from QCD itself. In all branches the submission answers the source question directly — existence or non-existence first, then location if existent — and phenomenological model estimates alone do not qualify, matching the source's demand for a first-principles study.
verification_standard: The submission is checked against the source-faithful question: does a QCD critical point exist, and if so at what critical temperature and density, from first principles. A submission passes if and only if it is one of the following, with each component reviewed as a separate checkable unit of the same problem: (1) Existence plus location — a first-principles QCD calculation that (a) establishes a critical endpoint with quantified critical temperature and density, (b) documents statistical and systematic uncertainties including continuum and volume control appropriate to the method, and (c) demonstrates that the sign problem at nonzero chemical potential is controlled within the claimed error budget; the existence conclusion and the $(T, \mu_B)$ values are checked as separate units. (2) Exclusion — a first-principles QCD calculation excluding a critical point over an explicitly stated region of the phase diagram, with the methodological control and uncertainties supporting that exclusion documented. (3) No-go — a rigorous proof establishing non-existence or an existence constraint from QCD. In every branch the reviewer verifies that the result is first-principles (phenomenological models alone fail), that no narrowing of the phase-diagram region or observable has been introduced to obtain a cheap check, and that the claimed conclusion follows under the stated control of errors. The standard does not prescribe which method may be used and does not redefine the question.
verification_difficulty_rationale: The result genuinely answers the source question only if the sign problem is demonstrably controlled, so the load-bearing derivations a reviewer must inspect are the validity of the submitter's finite-density method (which by necessity departs from standard, sign-problem-defeated techniques), the error analysis supporting the claimed existence/location or exclusion, and the continuum and volume extrapolations. Cheapest branch first: a rigorous no-go proof would be a long, novel natural-language derivation chain (high derivation-review burden, near-holistic), so it is not the cheapest branch. A simulation-based establishment allows delegating reruns of submitted code under a pinned protocol to reproduce quoted observables, but reproduction alone cannot settle the claim: the reviewer must still reconstruct why the method's treatment of the complex action is valid, check that uncertainty quantification covers the sign-problem-related systematics, and review substantial non-standard code for correctness rather than merely running it. That residual is a long, fragile, and novel connected chain, placing the score in the 7–9 band; 8 reflects that the method-validity and error-control arguments are mutually dependent and technique-novel, while bounded replay of the numerical pipeline removes part of the burden. The post-2022 literature does not change this assessment: even the strongest current constraint (Borsanyi et al. 2025) is community-scrutinized precisely over the validity of its continuation ansatz, illustrating that the method-validity review — not rerunning code — carries the burden. Limits that remain after review: results hold within the documented region, precision, and systematic budget; no branch can certify more than that. The score is descriptive metadata only and does not gate this high-importance problem.
solution_review_checklist: Confirm the submission is a first-principles QCD study; reject phenomenological-model-only answers per the source's explicit demand.
Check that the treatment of the complex action / sign problem at nonzero chemical potential is demonstrated to be controlled within the claimed error budget, not assumed away.
Verify continuum and finite-volume control appropriate to the method, and that quoted statistical and systematic uncertainties cover sign-problem-related systematics.

Review the existence conclusion and the quoted critical temperature and density as separate checkable units (branch 1), or the stated exclusion region and its confidence (branch 2), or the derivation chain from QCD assumptions (branch 3).
Confirm no narrowing of the phase-diagram region, observable, or answer form has been introduced to obtain a cheap check, and that the claimed conclusion follows under the stated error control.

Where numerical pipelines are submitted, rerun submitted analysis code on pinned inputs and compare quoted observables within stated tolerances, while treating code correctness and method validity as human-review items.
estimated_solution_review_time: Weeks to months of expert review: referee-level reading of the method-validity and error-control arguments plus bounded reruns of the submitted numerical pipeline; comparable to refereeing a landmark lattice-QCD or functional-QCD claim with independent cross-checks.
acceptance_boundary: Passes only as one of the three branches of the source question: a controlled first-principles establishment of the critical point with quantified $(T_E, \mu_B^E)$ and demonstrated sign-problem control; a controlled first-principles exclusion over an explicitly stated region; or a rigorous QCD-level no-go proof. Fails: phenomenological or holographic model estimates alone; results that assume away or leave unquantified the sign-problem systematics; experimental fluctuation signals alone without a first-principles determination; exclusions stated at weak confidence under a single untested continuation ansatz presented as full closure; and any answer that silently narrows the phase-diagram region or redefines the observable.
ci_pseudocode: Placeholder — no automated checker exists for this problem. A future checker could at most replay a submitted numerical pipeline: rerun the submitter's lattice or functional-QCD analysis code on pinned inputs and pinned statistics, recompute the quoted observables (e.g., entropy-density contours, cumulants, extrapolated critical coordinates), and compare against the submission within stated tolerances. The load-bearing judgments — validity of the complex-action treatment, adequacy of uncertainty quantification, and faithfulness to the source question — are derivation-review tasks that no named terminating procedure performs, so they remain with human reviewers.
ci_runner: none — no automated checker defined; human expert review only

evidence.title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
evidence.supports: Direct: full HTML text of the Nagata review inspected, including Section 1.1.1, which states verbatim that the QCD critical point 'has not been discovered so far', that 'even the very existence is not established', and that a first-principles QCD study is needed to establish existence or non-existence and, if it exists, the critical temperature and density. This is the authoritative formulation anchor for the named problem.

evidence.title: Lattice QCD constraints on the critical point from an improved precision equation of state
evidence.supports: Direct: abstract and listing inspected. Borsanyi et al. use a new continuum-extrapolated equation of state at zero density (lattices with $N_\tau=8,10,12,16$) plus new imaginary-chemical-potential data, following constant-entropy-density contours to real $\mu_B$ under strangeness neutrality, and exclude a critical point at $\mu_B < 450$ MeV at the $2\sigma$ level. This is the strongest current same-core lattice constraint: it narrows the viable region but is ansatz-dependent, statistically limited, and explicitly leaves existence at larger $\mu_B$ undecided — it does not close or definitively narrow the source question.

evidence.title: Precision Measurement of (Net-)proton Number Fluctuations in Au+Au Collisions at RHIC (STAR Collaboration, Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 142301 (2025))
evidence.supports: Direct: abstract and collaboration summary material inspected. BES-II precision cumulants and factorial cumulants of (net-)protons at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=7.7\text{--}27$ GeV show deviations from several non-critical baselines at $2\text{--}5\sigma$ (net-proton $C_4/C_2$ minimum near 19.6 GeV); the collaboration's public summary states the data rule out a critical point in regions accessed at top RHIC and LHC energies while leaving lower collision energies open. Experimental evidence narrows the viable region but is baseline-model-dependent and cannot, per the source's first-principles demand, settle the question either way.

evidence.title: Phase Transitions in Particle Physics: Results and Perspectives from Lattice Quantum Chromo-Dynamics (Aarts et al., Prog. Part. Nucl. Phys. 133, 104070 (2023))
evidence.supports: Direct: substantial text excerpts inspected. The review surveys all major sign-problem approaches (Taylor expansion, reweighting, complex Langevin, Lefschetz thimbles, density of states, analytic continuation, canonical ensemble) for first-principles study of the QCD critical endpoint and states that none of them provides the final solution to the sign problem, confirming the continuing-open status of the same core one year after the source review.

evidence.title: Searching for the QCD critical endpoint using multipoint Padé approximants (Clarke et al., Phys. Rev. D 112, L091504 (2025))
evidence.supports: Supplementary: citation-level record from multiple 2025–2026 papers' reference lists. A concurrent lattice effort searching for the critical endpoint via multipoint Pade resummation of Taylor coefficients; its existence as an ongoing search (rather than a claimed discovery or exclusion) corroborates that the same core remains open on the lattice front.

evidence.title: Lattice Study of Critical Point and Roberge-Weiss Phase Transition in Heavy-Quark Region of QCD (Wada, Kitazawa, Kanaya; Phys. Rev. Lett. 134, 162302 (2025))
evidence.supports: Supplementary: citation and talk-level record inspected. Studies critical-point structure in the heavy-quark region of the QCD phase diagram (the quark-mass direction, near the Roberge-Weiss endpoint), a different and more tractable corner than the physical-mass finite-$\mu_B$ critical point of the source question; it does not bear on existence or location of the physical QCD critical point.

evidence.title: Search for the QCD Critical Point in High Energy Nuclear Collisions: A Status Report (Zhang, Wang, Luo, Xu, 2026)
evidence.supports: Supplementary: citation-level record from a 2026 paper's reference list. A 2026 status report on the experimental critical-point search, cited as current in 2026 literature, corroborating that the community continues to treat the critical-point existence and location as an unresolved experimental and theoretical target rather than a settled one.
